aathira varier Mumbai, 3 November Banks need to ensure appropri- ate risk pricing, sound under- writing and a clear assessment of borrowers’ repayment capacity to sustain growth, Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Deputy Governor Swaminathan J said. Delivering a speech at the Leadership Conference of Indian Bank in Chennai last month, he emphasised that a stable and diversiﬁed deposit franchise is equally important to support credit expansion. The speech was uploaded on the RBI website on Tuesday. Swaminathan said one of the most valuable contributions of senior management is to identify talent, entrust people with responsibility and prepare them to exercise independent judge- ment. “This involves more than formal succession planning. It requires creating opportun- ities for younger colleagues to take initiative, learn from experience and develop the conﬁdence to lead.” Growth is essential to the banking sector’s role in suppor- ting India’s economic develop- ment, but it must be balanced, appropriately funded and con- sistent with long-term institu- tional strength, he said. “Growth remains essential to the banking sector’s role in supporting India’s economic development. How- ever, its sustainability depends on sound underwriting, appro- priate risk pricing, and a clear understanding of borrowers’ repayment capacity,” he said. Swaminathan also high- lighted how changing household savings preferences and greater choices among ﬁnancial prod- ucts were altering the environ- ment for deposit mobilisation. Banks now operate within a wider ﬁnancial ecosystem com- prising ﬁntech companies, tech- nology platforms and other service providers, creating new opportunities for collaboration while changing competitive dynamics. He said technological devel- opments, including digital payments, artiﬁcial intelligence and advances in data analytics, were reshaping banking and cus- tomer expectations. Banks needed to harness these techno- logies to improve customer experience, operational effi- ciency and competitiveness. The deputy governor also stressed that operational and technological resilience had become as important as credit and market risk. Cybersecurity, data protection, business con- tinuity and effective oversight of third-party service providers must be integral to institutional planning, he said. He also emphasised the importance of governance, transparency, internal controls and accou ntability, along with responsible lending, fair customer treatment and effec- tive grievance redressal to main- tain public conﬁdence. “Governance must be reﬂected not only in policies and procedures, but also in the quality of decisions taken throughout the institution. Clear accountability, effective internal controls, transparency and a willingness to identify and address emerging issues are essential. Responsible lending, fair customer treatment, and effective grievance redressal remain central to public conﬁ- dence. Ultimately, an institu- tion’s reputation is built on how consistently it fulﬁls its responsi- bilities to customers and other stakeholders,” he said. The banking system, he said, was approaching the task of pre- paring for future challenges from a position of strength, with improvements in asset quality, capital adequacy and proﬁtability providing a sound foundation. Swaminathan also called on bank leaders to invest in developing talent, encourage dif- fering viewpoints and prepare younger employees for leader- ship responsibilities, saying institutional strength must extend beyond the tenure of individual leaders. According to Swaminathan, the legacy of leadership extends bey ond business achievements or individual milestones. It lies in the quality of the institution handed ov er to those who follow — its peo ple, its systems, its values and its capacity to meet future challenges. “A leader’s most enduring achievement may well be an insti- tution that continues to grow stronger long after the leader has moved on,” he added. Proper risk pricing, sound underwriting crucial to sustainable growth: RBI dy guv RBI eases reporting norms for small service exporters and importers The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on Tuesday eased reporting requirements for small service exporters and importers, including relaxing rules for ﬁling export declarations. The central bank has made amendments to the Foreign Exchange Management (Export and Import of Goods and Services) Regulations. Under the revised norms, the exporter of services will be deemed to have submitted the export declaration form when they furnish the necess- ary information regarding receipt of payment to an auth- orised dealer for crediting their accounts. For exporters other than resident individuals, the same facility will be available for inward remittances of up to ~10 lakh, or its equivalent in foreign currency, for a service. The RBI has also eased the import data processing and monitoring system (IDPMS) reporting requirements for service imports, subject to spe- ciﬁc conditions. Under the amended regula- tions, authorised dealer banks will be required to enter details of service imports in the IDPMS within ﬁve working days of receiving the informa- tion only in cases where the importer is not a resident indi- vidual and the invoice or contract value exceeds ~10 lakh, or its equivalent in for- eign currency. The revised norms have come into effect retrospec- tively from October 1, 2026. pti (governance must be reflected not only in policies and procedures, but also in the quality of decisions taken throughout the institution) Swaminathan J Deputy governor of RBI
